<reason>Both sides argued competently, but CON built a more decisive, cumulative case. CON's pressure questions forced PRO to concede twice that no validated criterion distinguishes true persisters from adolescents whose identity might shift, and CON then converted that concession into a sharp "fork" argument in Rebuttal 2: PRO's benefit evidence comes from cohorts who completed hormones, not from a validated "persistent" subpopulation, so PRO cannot claim its outcome data attaches to the motion's specific "carefully screened" group. PRO's responses (reframing blockers as already constituting "access," insisting screening still serves a filtering function even without predictive certainty) were reasonable but never squarely resolved this mismatch, and PRO's closing repeated the "screening reduces error" line without directly rebutting the evidentiary-population problem CON isolated. CON's closing crystallized the clash cleanly around burden of proof, which is the correct decision rule for this motion. CON's case did suffer an execution cost: both its opening and second rebuttal were clipped for exceeding the word limit, cutting off the ends of otherwise strong arguments, which is a real format penalty. Even accounting for that, CON's substantive rebuttal work was sharper, more responsive to PRO's specific concessions, and better focused the debate on the actual comparison the motion demands.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 [B4.1]: pointing out that PRO's cited benefit evidence comes from adolescents who completed hormone treatment, not from a validated cohort of "true persisters," directly exploiting PRO's own admission that no such validated screening criterion exists.</best_rebuttal>
